title: Education as a collective practice.
intro: A space for education, thought and political discussion.
body:
Orsini grows out of the need for a stable space for education, thought and political discussion, able to take a critical look at the social, cultural and economic transformations of the present. It stands halfway between a study centre and a space for public intervention: a place where reading and theoretical education are not ends in themselves, but tools for understanding the present, building our own positions and opening new fields of action.

At a time marked by a proliferation of public debates, the fragmentation of political communities and the growing conversion of critical thought into identity, opinion or cultural product, Orsini wants to reclaim education as a collective practice. Against the fast consumption of discourse, it offers time to read, discuss, weigh up positions and build arguments. Against an endless succession of topical debates, it seeks to build frameworks that allow us to intervene in them more deeply.

In a city that already offers a wide range of talks and seminars, Orsini does not aim to be one more lecture programme or a string of unconnected courses. Its goal is to build, step by step, a stable community of learning, research and discussion bringing together researchers, writers, activists, cultural workers and anyone interested in acquiring tools to understand and act on the present. In doing so, it hopes to help train new political cadres and to set lines of debate.

## Reading, discussion and producing content

At first, Orsini’s main activity will be organised around short courses of five or six sessions. Each course will start from a clearly defined problem, a tradition of thought, or one or more books that provide a common framework for discussion.

Groups will be small —around fifteen participants— to keep the sessions participatory. Each course will have a person responsible for its design and follow-up, and may bring in invited researchers, writers, activists or specialists.

Alongside these regular programmes, Orsini may organise intensive courses, reading groups and seminars on current debates, or take advantage of authors and thinkers passing through Barcelona to address specific questions. Activities related to READ may also be explored.

The programme will offer different levels of involvement: you can take part as an auditor, following the sessions and readings, or take a more demanding path including exercises, your own written work, tutorials, assessment and follow-up. Where it makes sense, the core reading materials may be included in the registration.

Courses will end with a participatory session devoted to sharing work, hypotheses, materials or conclusions, so that the knowledge produced flows not only from those who teach to those who take part, but also among the participants themselves.

## Building communities of thought and action

Orsini’s horizon goes beyond offering a yearly calendar of activities: the aim is for the different courses to gradually form a stable community and to connect progressively with one another.

In a first stage, around five courses a year are planned, with roughly fifteen participants each. This scale makes it possible to experiment with formats, consolidate audiences and identify lines of interest before expanding the structure.

In the medium term, several courses could be grouped into thematic pathways or longer programmes. Five related courses, for example, could add up to a pathway comparable in intensity to a postgraduate programme, combining the flexibility of standalone courses with learning processes sustained over time.

At the same time, we will explore collaboration with educational institutions to offer academic recognition or credits, without letting accreditation constrain—at least initially—the intellectual and experimental freedom of the project.

## Why Orsini?

Orsini takes its name from the bomb designed by the Italian revolutionary Felice Orsini and used in the attempt on the life of Napoleon III in 1858. Decades later, the device became tied to the history of Barcelona through the 1893 bombing of the Liceu opera house, one of the most dramatic episodes of social conflict in the city.

The name recalls the memory of the “Rose of Fire”, the rebellious working-class Barcelona that, between the late nineteenth century and the first decades of the twentieth, became one of the great centres of world revolution. A history shaped by exploitation, social struggle and repression, but also by the building of unions, ateneus, schools and newspapers that turned culture and education into tools of emancipation.

Jacques Rancière questions “the age-old hierarchy that subordinates those who work with their hands to those who have been granted the privilege of thought”. In his book *La nuit des prolétaires* he studies workers who spent the hours meant for rest reading, writing and arguing, thereby challenging the separation between those who work and those who have the “privilege” of thinking. Calling this project Orsini takes up that tradition of working-class self-education: winning time for study, recognising ourselves as capable of producing thought, and building with others a life that overflows the place we have been assigned.
